{{Short description|Open specification for a metadata layer that turns files in object storage into a database-like table}}

An '''open table format''' is an [[open standard|open specification]] for a
metadata layer that organizes a collection of data files in
[[cloud storage|object storage]] into a single logical table, adding
database-like guarantees such as [[ACID]] transactions, [[schema evolution]],
and point-in-time ("time travel") queries. Open table formats sit above open
[[file format]]s such as [[Apache Parquet]] and below the query engines and
[[data catalog]]s that read and write the data, and they are a foundational
storage layer of the [[data lakehouse]] architecture.<ref name="isurvey">{{cite journal |title=Data Lakehouse: A survey and experimental study |journal=Information Systems |volume=127 |year=2024 |doi=10.1016/j.is.2024.102460}}</ref>

The most widely used open table formats are [[Delta Lake]], [[Apache Iceberg]],
and Apache Hudi, together with the more recent Apache Paimon. They emerged
between roughly 2016 and 2020 to bring the reliability and management features
of a [[data warehouse]] to the low-cost, open storage of a
[[data lake]].<ref name="isurvey" /><ref name="cidr2023">{{cite conference |title=Analyzing and Comparing Lakehouse Storage Systems |conference=Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR) |year=2023 |url=https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2023/papers/p92-jain.pdf}}</ref>

== Concept and motivation ==

A [[data lake]] stores data as files in object storage, typically in open
columnar formats such as [[Apache Parquet]] or ORC. A file format defines how
the bytes of an individual file are laid out, but it does not define which files
make up a table, nor does it coordinate concurrent readers and writers. Early
conventions such as [[Apache Hive]] tables tracked table membership through
directory layout, which made operations like updating rows, changing a table's
schema, or reading a table while it was being written unreliable.<ref name="cidr2023" />

An open table format addresses this by maintaining a separate metadata layer
that records the exact set of files belonging to each version of a table. This
lets engines commit changes atomically and read a consistent view of the table
while it is being written. It also lets a table's schema and partitioning change
over time without rewriting existing data. Because the specification and the
data are both open, multiple independent engines can read and write the same
table.<ref name="isurvey" /><ref name="cidr2023" />

== How they work ==

Although the formats differ in detail, they share a common model: a metadata
layer tracks which data files constitute each committed version, or ''snapshot'',
of a table. Reading a table means resolving the current snapshot to a list of
files; writing means producing new data files and then atomically committing new
metadata that points to them. Retaining older snapshots enables time-travel
queries and rollback, and comparing snapshots supports incremental
processing.<ref name="cidr2023" /><ref name="isurvey" />

== Major formats ==

'''[[Delta Lake]]''' was developed at [[Databricks]] and released as open source
in 2019; it was later contributed to the [[Linux Foundation]]. It stores table
metadata in a transaction log kept alongside the Parquet data files.<ref name="tc2019">{{cite web |last=Lardinois |first=Frederic |title=Databricks brings its Delta Lake open source project to the Linux Foundation |work=[[TechCrunch]] |date=2019-10-15 |url=https://techcrunch.com/2019/10/15/databricks-brings-its-delta-lake-open-source-project-to-the-linux-foundation/}}</ref>

'''[[Apache Iceberg]]''' was started at [[Netflix]] by Ryan Blue and Dan Weeks
in 2017, donated to the [[Apache Software Foundation]] in November 2018, and
became a top-level Apache project in May 2020.<ref name="icebergasf">{{cite web |title=Apache Iceberg |publisher=Apache Software Foundation |url=https://iceberg.apache.org/}}</ref><ref name="icebergincubator">{{cite web |title=Apache Iceberg — Project Incubation Status |publisher=Apache Software Foundation |url=https://incubator.apache.org/projects/iceberg.html}}</ref>
In June 2024, Databricks acquired Tabular, a company founded by Iceberg's
original creators, in a deal reported at over US$1&nbsp;billion (later reported
at about US$2&nbsp;billion), saying it wanted to move Delta Lake and Iceberg
toward a common standard.<ref name="cnbctabular">{{cite web |title=Databricks is buying data optimization startup Tabular |work=[[CNBC]] |date=2024-06-04 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/06/04/databricks-is-buying-data-optimization-startup-tabular.html}}</ref><ref name="tctabular2b">{{cite web |title=Databricks reportedly paid $2 billion in Tabular acquisition |work=[[TechCrunch]] |date=2024-08-14 |url=https://techcrunch.com/2024/08/14/databricks-reportedly-paid-2-billion-in-tabular-acquisition/}}</ref>

'''Apache Hudi''' (from "Hadoop Upserts Deletes and Incrementals") originated at
[[Uber]] around 2016 to support efficient row-level upserts and incremental data
ingestion, and later became an Apache Software Foundation project.<ref name="uberhudi">{{cite web |title=Apache Hudi at Uber: Engineering for Trillion-Record-Scale Data Lake Operations |work=Uber Engineering Blog |url=https://www.uber.com/en-US/blog/apache-hudi-at-uber/}}</ref>
'''Apache Paimon''' began as Flink Table Store within the [[Apache Flink]]
project and entered the Apache incubator in 2023, where it was renamed; it is
designed as a streaming-first lake format.<ref name="paimonflink">{{cite web |title=What is Paimon (incubating) (formerly Flink Table Store)? |publisher=Apache Software Foundation |url=https://flink.apache.org/what-is-flink-table-store/}}</ref>

== Interoperability ==

Because several formats coexist, tools have emerged to translate between them.
Apache XTable (formerly OneTable) provides omni-directional translation of table
metadata among Hudi, Delta Lake, and Iceberg without rewriting the underlying
data files.<ref name="siunif">{{cite web |title=Databricks' Delta Lake 3.0 bridges compatibility gaps with Apache Iceberg and Hudi |work=SiliconANGLE |date=2023-06-28 |url=https://siliconangle.com/2023/06/28/databricks-delta-lake-3-0-bridges-compatibility-gaps-apache-iceberg-hudi/}}</ref>
Databricks' UniForm, introduced with Delta Lake 3.0 in 2023, lets a Delta table
also expose Iceberg- and Hudi-compatible metadata over a single copy of the
data.<ref name="siunif" /> By the mid-2020s, some reporting described the formats
as converging rather than competing.<ref name="regcollide">{{cite web |last=Clark |first=Lindsay |title=Delta Lake and Iceberg communities collide – in a good way |work=[[The Register]] |date=2025-04-15 |url=https://www.theregister.com/2025/04/15/iceberg_delta_lake_collab/}}</ref>
